newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS STAR BECKER PLANS TO RAISE FAMILY IN U.S..
newsitem.headline: TENNIS STAR BECKER PLANS TO RAISE FAMILY IN U.S..

text.p: Tennis star Boris Becker said in a television interview on Sunday he wanted to raise his three-year-old son in the United States because the boy had almost no chance of a normal life in Germany.
"The price I pay for my fame and success is my private life," Becker, the world number two tennis player, said in a taped interview on the SAT1 network from his house in Florida.
"I can handle that for myself. But my son, it is not his fault he is my son. It is very unpleasant for me and my wife that he is so famous for no reason."
Becker, 29, said he wanted to move his family to the United States in about three years' time, when he son Noah started school, to escape the enormous celebrity pressures in Germany.

He said he and his wife, who is black, believed their son would be able to lead a more normal life in a multi-racial society. "We have a giant responsibility for him in that he grows up as freely as he can," he said.

"At the moment, he isn't free. In Munich, people handle him too well or badly if they are envious. It is difficult enough to grow up with dark skin if your friends are white and the society is white. We really want to see that we create an environment for him where skin colour is not important."

Becker said he was proud to be German and liked living in Munich, but he enjoyed spending time in Florida because he could move about freely without protection from the fans who mob his every public appearance in Germany.
"I feel extremely comfortable here," said Becker, who was depicted in the broadcast jogging on the beach and watching a Miami Heat basketball game without being asked for autographs.
"I can be myself here. I don't feel like I am being watched here. That doesn't work like that in Germany. I can cheer loudly here (at basketball games) and say what I want. It's a lot of fun."
Becker said he was also growing weary of threats in Germany sent to him because of his high income.

"It always happens when I playing a lot in Germany, when I am in TV a lot there, and there are lots of reports how much money I earn, or allegedly earn People always forget that I have to pay 50 percent of that (in taxes)," he said.

"Suddenly, the crazies start coming out of the holes and start writing threatening letters. It is really bad and that is where I start wondering if it is still worth it, if the price of fear is not too high."

Becker recalled that he was recently driven to a training session with five cars filled with bodyguards. "It was like a bad detective series," he said. "I was sitting there thinking to myself: this is insane."
